pronunciation.approximation: ah-SKLAY-pee-OSS, with the stress on the ultima and a long ē.
pronunciation.note: Attic Ἀσκληπιός places the acute on the final syllable; the η is unambiguously long, so the stacked macron-acute of the ideal form ḗ is philologically defensible. The owned form Asklēpiós follows the house rule against stacked marks while preserving both features across two characters.

domains.title: The Physician of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Medicine, Healing, Incubation, and the Boundary of Death
domains.lead: Asklēpiós is the only hero whose skill frightened the gods: the surgeon-son of Apóllōn who healed so well that Zeús destroyed him for emptying the underworld. His sanctuaries were the hospitals of the ancient world, and his snake-entwined staff still hangs over every pharmacy on earth.

cards.name: The Rod
cards.desc: A single serpent on a staff — the true emblem of medicine, distinct from Hermês' two-snaked caduceus.

cards.name: Epidaurus

cards.name: Incubation

cards.name: The Thunderbolt
cards.desc: Zeús' answer to resurrection — the line past which even healing becomes transgression.

mythology.lead: Born from catastrophe — cut from the womb of the dying Korōnis by his father Apóllōn — Asklēpiós was raised by the centaur Cheirōn, who taught him the pharmaka of roots and the surgery of the knife.

myths.title: The Child of the Pyre
myths.text: Korōnis, daughter of Phlegyas, lay with Apóllōn and bore his child — and then, ‘in the error of her heart’, loved a mortal, Ischys of Arcadia. A raven brought the news to Delphi, and Apóllōn, in the grip of his godhead, sent his sister to deal death while the girl already lay on her father’s pyre. From the flames the god himself snatched the unborn infant (Pindar, Pythian 3.1–46; Apollodorus 3.10.3). The child was given to Cheirōn, the wise centaur of Pelion, who reared him on the mountain’s roots and simples — and Pausanias (2.26.6) records the Arcadian variant in which no fire was needed: the babe was exposed and found by a goat and a dog, his first nurses and his first patients. Pindar builds the whole ode as a warning around the birth: even the god’s beloved could not escape her own choice. The myth’s meaning is surgical — the greatest healer of antiquity begins his career on the table, rescued from death by the father whose arrows also caused it.

myths.title: Raising the Dead
myths.text: From Athēnā, Asklēpiós received the blood of the Gorgōn Medousa — half of it a poison that kills, half a pharmakon that restores the dead (Apollodorus 3.10.3). He used the saving half. Pausanias records the tradition that he raised Hippolytos, the prince cursed by Aphrodítē, and that the grateful Troezenians thereafter thanked the god as ‘the one raised from the dead’ (2.27.4); Diodorus (4.71), more cynical, says he grew rich charging fees for resurrections, until Hāidēs complained of an empty kingdom. Zeús settled the matter with the thunderbolt: the healer who unmade death had unmade the order that made healing necessary. Apóllōn avenged his son by killing the Kyklōpes who forge Zeús’ bolts, served a year of penance in Admetos’ house, and at last Zeús raised Asklēpiós among the stars (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.534–632). The myth draws medicine’s oldest line in the sand, and the ancients walked it openly: to cure for a fee is piety, to resurrect for a fee is hubris.

myths.title: The Sleep that Cures
myths.text: The sanctuaries turned the god’s art into an institution. At Epidaurus the sick underwent purification — baths, fasting, abstinence from wine — then slept in the abaton, the ‘place of not-walking’, waiting for the god (Pausanias 2.26–27). He came in a dream, or sent his animals: the sacred dogs that licked wounds — Aristophanes stages one licking a blind man’s eyes in the Plutus (653–747) — and the harmless serpents whose touch was diagnosis. Morning brought the priests’ interpretation, diet, regimen, and sometimes surgery; the cures were inscribed on marble, the iamata (IG IV² 1, 121–124), and some seventy survive: a man with an arrowhead in his jaw dreams the god extracts it and wakes holding it; a pregnant sleeper is delivered in her dream and wakes holding her newborn. However one weighs miracle against medicine, the system worked — the sanctuary grew into the ancient world’s greatest hospital complex, with a theatre where patients watched drama as therapy. Dream became the first diagnostic instrument, and the temple the first hospital.

myths.title: A Cock for Asklēpiós
myths.text: Plato records the last words of Sócrates in the Phaedo (118a). The hemlock had done its work, and the philosopher lifted the covering from his face: ‘Krítōn, we owe a cock to Asklēpiós; pay it, and do not neglect it.’ A cock — the vigil-bird, the traditional thank-offering of the healed. The sentence has been turned over ever since: was Sócrates thanking the god for the cure of a life? Ironizing his judges? Marking philosophy’s debt to the healer of bodies? The ancients themselves read it both piously and ironically, and the crux survives every exegesis. What is beyond argument is the offering’s ordinariness: the greatest mind of the city dies owing a chicken, exactly like any farmer cured of a fever. Asklēpiós’ last appearance in Greek literature is a reminder that his economy ran on small, precise debts — and that even death, in his books, could be entered as a treatment successfully concluded.

lore.syncretism: Rome imported him wholesale during the plague of 293 BCE: the Sibylline Books prescribed his cult, an embassy sailed to Epidaurus, and the god came as a snake — boarding the Roman ship at Antium, coiling on the mast, and gliding ashore on the Tiber Island, where his temple rose within the year in the shape of a ship (Livy 10.47; Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.622–744, makes the snake’s journey the centrepiece of his Roman aetiology). The identification stuck for a millennium: the island still serves the sick. In Egypt the traffic ran the other way — Greeks identified the deified vizier Imhotep, whose healing cult flourished at Saqqāra and Memphis, as ‘the Egyptian Asklēpiós’, and Ptolemaic pilgrims left Greek dedications in his galleries. Through every translation the god kept his instrument: the single snake on the single staff, medicine’s signature in two civilizations.
lore.culturalLegacy: His Rod — one snake, one staff — is the emblem of the World Health Organization, the American Medical Association, and thousands of medical schools, endlessly confused with the two-snaked caduceus of Hermês, a confusion institutionalized when the United States Army Medical Corps adopted the wrong staff in 1902. His sanctuary line ran unbroken into medicine’s institutions: the Hippocratic school grew up inside his temple at Kos, Galen served his cult at Pergamon before writing the ancient world’s greatest medical corpus, and the Hippocratic Oath itself opens by swearing ‘by Apóllōn the physician and Asklēpiós’ — the healer’s name is the second word of the profession’s oldest contract. His name still titles hospitals, journals, and medical software the world over. If any pagan god can be said never to have died, it is the son of Apóllōn: every pharmacy sign on earth is his votive offering, renewed nightly in neon.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Asklēpiós is the god of the second opinion. He stands at the exact border between what may be cured and what must be accepted, and the thunderbolt that killed him marks medicine’s eternal question — not whether we can, but whether we should. Every healer who has ever weighed a risk against a hope has stood inside his sanctuary; every patient who has slept waiting for an answer has kept the old vigil under other names.

His instruments are modest for a deity: a stick, a snake, a dog, a dream. No lightning, no trident — the tools of walking, shedding, watching, sleeping, the four ordinary miracles on which all healing secretly depends. The iamata taught the ancient world to record outcomes; the cock teaches the modern one that gratitude has a price, small and exact, and that it should be paid.

lore.archaeology: Epidaurus is the crown: a UNESCO World Heritage sanctuary preserving the abaton, the great theatre, and the circular tholos — the labyrinthine building Pausanias (2.27.3) attributes to Polykleitos the Younger, possibly the god’s ritual ‘dance floor’. The iamata stelai (IG IV² 1, 121–124) are the largest surviving archive of ancient patient testimony. At Kos the terraced Asklepieion climbs the hill behind the plane tree said to shade Hippocrates; at Pergamon, Galen’s home sanctuary, the great altar overlooked the healing terraces. In Rome the Tiber Island temple is gone, but its memory is carved in travertine: the island’s embankment still wears the relief prow of the ship that brought the god. Across all his shrines, the humblest artifacts speak loudest — thousands of terracotta votives shaped like the body parts the god had healed, hung on his walls like a catalogue of gratitude in clay.
